How to optimize fallout 3 for windows 7, 8, 8.1, and 10

Step 1: Run as Administartor
     Go to your Fallout 3 install folder within Steam. 
     Default location: C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Fallout 3 goty.
     Right click the Fallout 3 application file and select Properties.
     Select the Compatibility tab and tick the Run this program as an administrator box.

Step 2: Run fallout 3 in compatibility mode
     Go to your Fallout 3 install folder within Steam. 
     Default location: C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Fallout 3 goty.
     Right click the Fallout 3 application file and select Properties.
     Select the Compatibility Tab and check the box that says Run this program in compatibility mode for:.  
     Check the drop down box and troubleshoot with different Windows versions.
     Optionally, you can try compatibility with Windows XP SP3 .
     Click Apply and OK

Step 3: Edit your Fallout.ini file
     Open your My Documents folder.
     Under My Games, open the Fallout 3 folder and select the fallout.ini file.
     In the fallout.ini file, find the following line: bUseThreadedAI=0.
     Change this line to read: bUseThreadedAI=1.
     Add another line after it that reads: iNumHWThreads=2.
     Run the game.

I've been pretty burnt out on Open World games lately. Every time I look at one I feel like I've played it already, but I've had an urge to come back to Fallout 3 and after spending the week on it it I think I've realized it's not open world games that are the problem so much as it is [i]bad[/i], paint-by numbers open-world games with no substance. The thing that's struck me the most revisiting Fallout 3 is that nothing feels like filler. Where other games treat their world as a backdrop for a series of samey shootouts, Fallout 3 is a living, breathing world that you can actually [i]explore[/i]. In most games, buildings are just props to drive by, but in Fallout 3 you can enter almost every building you see, and you'll always find something interesting, be it loot, enemies, or even a little story that plays out independent of any quests. If you see something interesting in the distance, you can go there and there's something waiting for you.

Best embodying this "no-filler" philosophy is are the quests and side-quests. I recently played both Batman: Arkham Origns and Ubisoft's The Division, and the side-quests in those games amounted to "go here on the map, fight 2 or 3 guys". They're enjoyable in their way, but there's no depth to them. Every side-mission in Fallout 3 on the other hand, is a [i]story[/i]. You'll meet characters, go to unique locations, and actually engage with what you're doing.  Each mission is unique and it's refreshing to play a game where the quests actually had some thought and craftsmanship instead of the literal copy-and-paste game design that's become the lead standard for this genre. My least favorite thing about open world games is the prevalence of collectibles as the main side-mission and Fallout 3 doesn't waste your time on that nonsense. While the game does have collectable bobbleheads that boost your stats, it never even tells you about them and they're treated more like an easter egg than anything else, and unlike most games you actually have to search for them and strategize if you should even get them now or wait for later.

The high engagement with exploration and interaction also makes the world feel alive. Fallout 3 doesn't really hand you anything but instead places a series breadcrumbs for you to pick up on. You might see a scuffle playing out and meet a new faction naturally rather than the game introducing them through some big cutscene. Sometimes people just say things or you'll hear something on the radio and might go check it out. It can be a bit to keep track of, but it's immersive and makes you feel like a small part of a living, breathing world. While the graphics aren't the best on a technical level, the the Capitol Wasteland is [i]evocative[/i]. It probably helps that I live close to Washington DC and I love seeing something familiar to me, but this is really one of the best environments in a game. Washington looks properly [i]brutal[/i] and wandering around at night surrounded by monsters with 30's Jazz standards blaring is an eerie, atmospheric experience. There are plenty of little settlements with a lot of life in them, but you always get the sense that they're little pockets of safety holding the world at bay rather than anything thriving, even if the inhabitants are doing comparatibely well.

None of that worldbuilding would matter if the game itself wasn't fun. While the gunplay can certainly be clunky in places, and you'll definitely see something weird even with the bugfixes, it's a blast leveling up and grinding enemies into a fine paste and I truly enjoy the combat. I always focus on guns early on and while the early game is challenging, it's also fair. Fallout 3 has kind of a reverse difficulty curve where you become much better at killing common enemies, but the power trip is part of the fun and each level gives you a really tangible increase in your abilities. They also start throwing some stronger enemies in the mix, so there's always a challenge if you look for it it regardless of how powerful you are.

While some may prioritize Fallout New Vegas over Fallout 3 due to having a bigger world, some additional gameplay features, and a stronger overarching plot, 3 is an excellent game with a ton of depth and I feel like it has a bleaker, more desolate vision of apocalypse that really resonates with me. The base game here is huge, and there's a ton more to get out of DLC. The 75 hours on this review isn't even close to the real time I've spent on Fallout 3, as I played a lot before steam even tracked time and you have to launch the game through a mod-loader to use the fix patch which doesn't track time. It does take effort to get everything up-and-running but the payoff is one of the richest and most satisfying games of its genre.

[h1]Fallout 3: Game of the Year Edition.[/h1]
[i]When war changed.[/i]

Note: This review is about the game's content, not the instability on Win 7+. These problems are mentioned, but not central to the review.

Fallout 3 is a fantastic game, but also not quite what a Fallout game should be. It excels in the ways all [i]Bethesda[/i] games do; with its compelling open-world exploration, astute environmental storytelling, and immersive atmosphere, but falls short on several other marks. The roleplaying is just adequate, the characters are weak, and the writing of the main storyline is near-abysmal, despite all of these "mehs" and negatives being huge positives for the classic Fallout games and New Vegas. In the end Fo3 shakes out to be a remarkable experience, but I can't say I'm happy with where it lead this franchise.

Fallout 3 was the first Fallout game to be set on the East Coast, taking place in the bombed out ruins of D.C. and its surrounding rural regions of Virginia and Maryland. The introduction slideshow does a good job of explaining to new-comers how the world became a nuclear hell-scape, and if you'd like, you can watch that [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJcuAau2RKA]here.[/url] Otherwise, the opening stages are one big tutorial where your custom character is born and raised in a vault, which culminates in your father leaving said vault for unknown reasons, despite this being forbidden. You become a target of the tyrannical vault overseer due to this, and must escape to track down your father; this being your main quest.

Now that you have a concept of what the main quest is about, I'll refrain from any spoilers, but state that the writing of it is flat-out awful. Each successive stage of the main quest railroads you along a linear path, and seems to be more about the story of your father and his past than the one you can craft for yourself in-game. Supporting characters always make the important decisions on what to do next, and only at the very end does any sort of player choice get involved. Many central plot details are even borrowed straight from Fallout 2, such as the presence of the G.E.C.K. and The Enclave, making the storyline unnecessarily unoriginal. The only conciliation is that the locations visited along this main quest-line are intriguing and fun to explore, but that hardly makes up for the terrible narrative. I'll talk more later about how the writing in the rest of the game is better, but I loathe the main quest.

On a brighter note; though it's stripped down from how it used to be, the roleplaying in Fo3 is both functional and accessible. Skills and perks have been carried along from the classics to provide good character creation and progression; and little about your past and personality other than that you're a Vault Dweller is decided for you, so you're free to determine the majority of your characters story yourself. Roleplaying mechanics like the dialogue and karma systems aid this; dialogue being an extension of your personality and skills, and karma being a way to add consequences to your actions. The dialogue is a tad restrictive at times and the karma is too black and white in most circumstances, but overall the roleplaying systems and writing passes Fo3 as solid in the roleplaying department.

The quests and characters of Fallout 3 generally lack the depth of the West Coast games, but do add a lot to your time in the Capital Wasteland regardless. Side quests often have multiple ways to be completed, and how they are played depends on your stats and who you're roleplaying as. Quality among them vary, but there are 4 or 5 stand-out side quests, and none are particularly unenjoyable. The characters you interact with throughout these quests are sadly one-dimensional however, with only a select few personas having any identifiable backstory or personality traits.

One of the things Fallout 3 indisputably does best, is the design of its game world. The rural areas feel like a genuinely tattered wasteland, and the gothic architecture of downtown D.C. is overbearingly atmospheric and reminiscent of classic Fallout titles. Civilization and society itself is in a strangely tenuous state given 200 years has passed since the war, though this is probably to play up the more brazen post-apocalyptic theme. City hubs and trade caravans do still realistically dot the wastes though. Aesthetically and thematically, the world is very satisfying, resulting in some unparalleled exploration.

Fallout 3's map is filled with interesting locations to explore; the vast majority of which have something special for you do, see, or in most cases, fight. Environmental storytelling has a strong foothold in many of these places, with unique tales often being conveyed to you through each given setting. Even when you aren't anywhere specific, simply tromping around the remains of the tristate area - with your pip-boy on blast to all of the best tunes of the 1940's and 50's - is supremely enjoyable. Needless to say, the exploration in Fo3 is its premier feature, and makes up for many of the games shortcomings.

The combat you do while exploring, though full of variety and delightfully gratuitous in violence, is too clunky and dysfunctional not to harp on. The bullet spread of guns is ridiculously high, there are no iron sights, and the AI of all your enemies is laughably unintelligent. These drawbacks have become worse with time too, expect for maybe bullet spread, as V.A.T.S. - a gameplay mechanic allowing you to stop time and target specific body parts on your opponents - is a legitimate fighting alternative. Overall, the combat isn't too impressive though.

You're probably already aware that Fallout 3 is a b*tch to get working on modern OS's, so I'd recommend clicking [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=149946772]here[/url] if you're on anything newer that Vista. Fo3 is a broadly unstable game anyway though, and I still get crashes every hour or two. The world is filled with minor bugs as well, but nothing too serious. In terms of frame rate however, the game is very smooth. All in all on the performance... it's a Bethesda game, that's for sure.

This is a review for the GOTY version, so I should quickly mention the DLC. There are 5 expansions in total, 4 of which add new maps and quest-lines to explore and complete, while the remaining 1 offers several new quests, and the ability to play past the end of the awful main storyline. The full game is ~80-90 hours long, and each DLC provides about 3-6 hours of worthwhile content, though some are better than others. Mothership Zeta is my least favorite, and I like Point Lookout best, but this is subjective. I'd recommend getting them all in this edition, as each one complements the main game nicely.

Bethesda games are well known for their modability, and for good reason. There are thousands of mods on the [url=http://www.nexusmods.com/fallout3/?]Fo3 Nexus,[/url] which can alter essentially every aspect of the game. A multitude of the more minor gameplay and performance issues I’ve addressed can be fixed with mods, so I’d absolutely endorse using them to fix any issues. Bringing modding to the franchise was definitely one of Fo3's biggest achievements.

I know I've been disproportionately more negative about this game than I should have been, because I really do love Fallout 3. How I view the game comes down to priorities, and even though I prefer a Fallout game to be much more thoughtful, philosophical, and narrative-based, once I came to terms with the fact that that's not what Fo3 is, I was able to appreciate it for its better half; exploration, world, and atmosphere. It also helps that it retains some roleplaying expertise, as well as the true Fallout aesthetic; enough so that I still feel like I'm playing a Fallout game. And, I'd pity any mainline Fallout title that didn't make that effort...

Alright. [i]Fallout 3: Game of the Year Edition[/i] is done and dusted. I played this many times on console, but this was my first playthrough on PC. And for me, on an unmodded Steam Deck with the current version of Proton, and with no game mods, this ran immaculately. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3224579396

In fact, this may have been one of the best games I've played on the Deck performance wise. Which is crazy to me considering how often the game would freeze stutter and crash when I played it previously (on console). I had one instance of stuttering in Operation: Anchorage during the final push and another instance of stuttering in Mothership Zeta, but beyond that, I literally had zero stability issues and it ran at a consistent 60 FPS on maxed settings with an average of around 25% CPU usage. 

It took me forever to get around to buying and playing this on Steam due to its widely reported compatibility issues, but thankfully, those were nonexistent for me. The home screen for some reason wasn't gamepad compatible, but everything else was and the default settings were fine.

So, with that out of the way, I want to talk a bit about the experience itself. For one, this game still looks great. Does it show its age? Yes and no. Things like character models actually look better than they do in Skyrim and Fallout 4 for some reason. But they don't look modern of course. However, the world itself has aged very well. The audio is pretty legendary, and that will never change I'm sure.

The gameplay also holds up to modern games quite well. Gunplay is fun and VATS never disappoints. Early to mid game, I would recommend keeping a Dart Gun on you. It makes fighting things like Deathclaws much easier, especially if you use it to target legs. Once you get the Gauss Rifle though, you won't need the Dart Gun or much else lol. It does great damage AND typically knocks enemies down as well. Nearly game breaking in its OP-ness, but it's also incredibly satisfying.

Btw, special weapons aside, Deathclaws are still panic inducing and terrifying lol. They're the fastest, strongest and meanest things in the game, and they have a sixth sense for being able to find you. You could be forgiven if you scream like a child when one leaps at you.

Exploring the DC Wasteland is quite memorable, and I went into this playthrough with a clear agenda for what I wanted to do and see outside of the main story. Given how well written a lot of the side quests are, there's a lot of good times to be had. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3227056838

As far as the DLC goes, I'd recommend doing [b]Operation: Anchorage[/b] first. It's the easiest, and although it lacks any nods to loot whores, the final payoff includes the other nearly game breaking piece of gear in the game: the Chinese Stealth Armor. Once you acquire that, the world is your oyster. Especially if you've leveled up your stealth. Takes maybe three hours to complete and is basically set up as a corridor shooter. If it weren't for the armor though, I'd probably skip this DLC.

[b]The Pitt[/b] is probably the most heavily reliant on the morality system and the one with the largest grey area in that regard. The actual setting is cool and does feature the best melee weapon in the game should you be playing that way. You can roll through this in three to four hours, but it can also take longer depending on how thorough you are. Fairly easy overall.

[b]Mothership Zeta[/b] is the quirkiest DLC. You get abducted by aliens, but you and some other abductees rebel and eventually take over the ship lol. Features some good weapons and some excellent healing/repair items. It's probably the funniest DLC and is moderately challenging. It's also the one that probably takes the longest to complete due to how confusing certain activities can be to complete. I probably spent around six hours here.

[b]Point Lookout[/b] is the most difficult DLC, is at least partially inspired by Deliverance and Southern Comfort, has some good next tier versions of weapons you've probably been using a lot. It also has some cool story stuff, including an important item for concluding a Cthulhu story arc in the base game, and is also the largest DLC. You can definitely wrap up the quests in four to five hours, but you could also spend ten to fifteen hours running around seeing and looting everything.

[b]Broken Steel[/b] is an endgame DLC, so once you've finished the main story, this one kicks off. I honestly wrapped this up in about two hours, maybe a bit less. But you could potentially get eight-ish hours out of it depending on how you handle certain situations and how much you explore and loot. Personally, I already had more ammo and healing stuff than I'd ever be able to use, so I took a more direct approach with this DLC. It does tie a bow on the Fallout 3 story, and is definitely worth experiencing.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3229333793

So yeah, I was very glad to get one final playthrough in. It was still awesome in this age of gaming, and while not perfect, each individual aspect of this game holds up immaculately.

[h1][b]HOW TO RUN FO3 ON Win10 (WITHOUT MODS)[/b][/h1]
Due to the age of the game, FO3 isn't optimised to run on modern PCs with Win10 - the 2 most pertinent issues being the game crashing on launch (after the launch screen) and the game randomly freezing during gameplay. Having initially been put off by the seemingly complex issues surrounding the game, I've since found the most straightfoward way to solve these recurring problems and hopefully get FO3 running for you.

[b]1) Crash on Launch[/b]
The solution is to simply download and install Games for Windows LIVE - however Microsoft has since removed the official GFWL download from their site. Luckily, the latest version was backed up on this site by PC Gaming Wiki: https://community.pcgamingwiki.com/files/file/1012-microsoft-games-for-windows-live/

Install this, and you should be able to run FO3 no problem. (Note: if you want to take this a step further, you can then proceed to install GFWL disabler from NexusMods to remove the dependency on GFWL)

[b]2) Game Randomly Freezes During Gameplay[/b]
Essentially, no matter how many cores your PC may have, the game was only designed to utilise 2. Luckily, there is an extremely simple way to get around this by slightly modifying the FO3 .ini file.

Step 1: Locate your FO3 .ini file (usually found in Documents -> My Games -> Fallout3; It's a Configuration settings file named "Fallout").

Step 2: Open it up in Notepad and change the line [b]bUseThreadedAI=0[/b] to [b]bUseThreadedAI=1[/b].

Step 3: Add the line [b]iNumHWThreads=2[/b] beneath it, then save the changes.

Your game should no longer freeze randomly during gameplay.

This may not be a fix-all for all issues in the game, but from what I've seen, it does fix the most common problems. Just thought I'd share it with everyone to save you guys the trouble. Great game otherwise!

THIS GAME IS 100% PLAYABLE ON WINDOWS 10 WITH FEW FIXES, READ BELOW:

An excellent post-apocalyptic open world shooter-RPG, even after 13 years. Due to the games age and the developers lack of interest to update the game, the game is not optimised for windows 7 and later but only with a few small fixes, the game is 100% playable even on windows 10! I have been playing on win10 for 21 hours with only 1 (one) crash so far and that was at the 12 hours mark. Here is a guide how to get Fallout 3 GOTY working on win10:

1. Remember to enable your DLC's and set your options. To do this, simply open the game launcher (opens by default after the first installation), click "Data Files" on the menu and enable all checkboxes. After this set your options as you like from the "Options" menu.


2. Download the "Games for Windows LIVE Disabler" over at Nexus. Read the "readme" guide and install.
Drop the "exe" into the game's install folder and run it, selecting "Disable G4WL" and "Move DLCs".

This causes steam to not track your gameplay hours. You can fix this by going into the game installation directory and moving the "FalloutLauncher" executable to a different folder (I moved it to a folder on my desktop) and then renaming the "Fallout3" executable to "FalloutLauncher". This skips the launcher menu when you launch the game on steam.

Note: After this step, if your control/key-mapping changes in the game do not come into effect, you can undo the renaming-changes above, change the controls and then repeat the part above. DO NOT DELETE the original "FalloutLauncher" executable!


3. Download the  "Intel HD graphics Bypass package" over at Nexus. Read the "readme" guide and install.
The the "dll" goes into the game's install folder and the "ini" goes into "Documents / My Games / Fallout 3"


4. You need to force the game to run at 60 FPS for the physics, animations and game mechanics to work properly. Do not believe any "Fallout 3 uncapped framerate" guides, they will just ruin the game. Unfortunately using Nvidia Control Panel didn't work for me so I used "Guru3D RTSS Rivatuner Statistics Server" to force 60 FPS and it works perfectly. Download the "version 7.3.1 Final" from their website and install it. After this open the software and set the Framerate limi to 60. The software has to be on, in the background while you are playing for this to come to effect.

Lastly, you can change the games FOV by opening the console and writing for example: fov 90 90
This will change the fov to 90 on the pipboy (first number) and first person view (second number). You can set the values differently as you like.

Fallout 3 was released in Oct. of 2008 with the GotY edition coming out a year later.  Having been released at a difficult time in Fallout history, it was under a lot of scrutiny.  The original two Fallout games were developed by Interplay games, with the second being handled by a smaller subsidiary known as Black Isles Studio.  

The original Fallouts were turn based, isometric games whose fans would rabidly criticize FO3, which became the first 3d offering into the Fallout universe as Bethesda games would purchase the license from a financially strapped Interplay.  It’s largely been described as “Oblivion with guns”, and depending on which side of the fence you’re standing on, it’s a good thing or a bad thing.

FO3 would be followed up by the title Fallout New Vegas, which was more or less FO3 in a new world space with some new assets.  FONV was developed by Obsidian games, which was largely made up of employees from the same Black Isles studio that produced Fallout 2.

The Fallout universe takes place in the post, post apocalyptic year of 2277, in an alternate US timeline, where the microchip was never developed and instead, nuclear power shaped the world, ultimately resulting in its destruction in 2077 when China and the United States (along with an annexed Canada) went to war and no one is quite sure who fired first.  The world was devastated by a combination of radiation and a mutated virus known as FEV.

While FO3 takes place on the east coast, largely centered around the DC area, FONV returned to the West Coast where the original lore of FO1 & 2 took place.  This contributed to even more criticism of FO3 regarding both its use of lore and the complaint that it was too far removed from its RPG roots.

The switch to a 3D world space, not unlike Bethesda’s Elder Scrolls series of games, brought in a huge boost in sales that would further Bethesda’s reputation for “dumbing down” games.   In reality, it was a good business move that allowed them to cater to a much larger audience.

FO3 starts you off with a main quest that guides you through the basics of the game, but then releases you into an open world where you can go where you please and do what you want.  Every location tells a story, whether that be a short backstory read on a computer terminal, a collectible such as an official vault-tec bobblehead or a magazine to increase your stats, or an actual side quest.  Some of the characters have complex backstories rooted to the areas they live in, while others are simply day to day characters that have little bearing on what you’re doing.

Fallout offers a skill system like most RPG based games, and certain events in the game are driven by what skills you choose.  Things like Big Gun, or Small Gun skills will effect practical things like how well you’re able to hit your target, while things like Speech and Medicine might effect how well you interact with NPC’s.  Each common skill is governed by your base stats deemed S.P.E.C.I.A.L. (Strength, Perception, Endurance, Charisma, Intelligence, Agility, and Luck) which is straight out of the original Fallout Lore.   

Factions also exist, such as Slavers or the Brotherhood Outcasts, who will remember if you get on their bad side, but by and large the biggest directive for how your story will turn out is the Karma system.  You can choose to play as Good, Neutral, or Evil and your actions can effect the world accordingly.  The gun play in FO3 is simplistic, lacking true iron sights, but you can choose to go in guns blazing or stealth your way through just for the story depending on how you stat your character.

A fair criticism to FO3 was its insistence on following the theme of sacrifice right up until the games ending, which was largely unsatisfying and drew a ton of ire from all fans.  But the Broken Steel DLC, corrected that, and allowed for play beyond the final mission, along with adding an additional 10 player levels and many other difficulty changes to the game.  Certain enemies at higher levels become absolute bullet sponges, which you will find both challenging and annoying and to be honest, it could have been done better.

The Mothership Zeta DLC, I found good, but a bit long.  The Pitt DLC is a much better offering.  Operation Alaska introduces some powerful new equipment that you’ll want to get no matter your play style, and finally, Point Lookout takes you in a much more comedic direction with a large world space and some interesting characters.  Of course all the DLC’s come with the GotY edition.

The game does suffer from the occasional bug or crash, but considering its age, they're relatively few and far between and being that it's a PC game Bethesda gives you access to the debug console which allows you to fix a lot of the issues you could potentially encounter.

Overall, this is a satisfying game and a good introduction to the Fallout world that should make you want to go on to FONV, and Fallout 4.  The game is extremely cheap when bought on a Steam sale and is well worth it.  The game has a lot of replay value due to the different builds and Karma features and if you get tired with the stock game, being a Bethesda title, you have access to a whole new world of gameplay via mods.

It should be noted that this game is over a decade old, and was originally intended to run on Windows XP.  While the Steam Store has [u]multiple[/u] mentions of this and a disclaimer right by the shopping cart button, some gamers seem to overlook the fact that you may need to do some tweaking to get the game to run on Windows 7, 8, 8.1, or 10, but it WILL run.  You will have to add Windows Games Live support, tweak an .ini to enable multiple cores, and possibly some other changes.   There is a stickied post in the discussion forums that will guide you on getting it running.   As with all PC games, particularly older ones, sometimes some tweaking is in order depending on your system.

People sleep on Fallout 3 because New Vegas is the meme, but this game rocks and is in every way a valid entry into the series. Overall: 10/10
Probably my favorite game of all time, although I really liked Fallout: New Vegas for it's weapon and ammo variety I still preferred Fallout 3s' atmosphere, story and characters.

Concept: 10/10
You are born in an underground vault that's had no contact with the outside world for hundreds of years. Create your own unique character, male or female, and quickly escape to learn that the nuclear war from long ago has left a wasteland topside. With humanity struggling for survival, mutants occupying the DC ruins with a mysterious agenda, and the various irradiated creatures of the waste, the setting feels like "Fallout". Play how you want, investing in the skills you choose to develope your character to reflect your play style.

Graphics: 8/10
At the time the graphics were not bad, but not good either. I would give some leneincy to Bethesda however, considering how large and content rich their open world games are. Character models could be stiff as well, but I was able to overlook this because of the sheer variety of locations, items, people and creatures you interact with.

Sound: 9/10
One thing i'll always credit Bethesda for is having so much voiced dialogue. Every NPC has voiced dialogue despite their importance, greatly improving immersion. I was also impressed with the radio stations. Hours and hours of music and dialogue between several different radio stations made the long walks to new destinations less of a bore. As far as Audio effects go i'd say most were well done. Some guns didn't sound like they had enough "bang" to be realistic, but the energy weapons and melee sounds were entertaining.

Playability: 9/10
Amazingly customizable, even more so with mods. You can make your character look how you want, play how you want, and do what you want. Use the weapons and tactics you want to use. If you want to go off and explore 30 minutes into the game you can, and it's just as rewarding/interesting as following the main quest. I only knock a point off of this due to the many bugs/issues people had at the release of this game. While it's improved drastically, there is still the occasional crash, glitch, or corruption.

Entertainment: 10/10
There are literally hundreds of hours of fun to be had here. A lot of people complained about the main quest, but I found it to be interesting and more importantly, rewarding. The main quest however, is just a tiny piece of the games content. 90% of the entertainment can be found by just exploring on your own. The character customiztion enhances this, making a lot of interactions and situations unique to your character based on their skill set or decisions. 

Replayability: 10/10
The amount of customization options and content ensure that no two playthroughs are the same. I've made half a dozen characters and still discover new things in this wasteland...

Fallout 3: Game Of The Year Edition is a post-apocalyptic story-rich open-world R.P.G. developed by Bethesda Game Studios and published by Bethesda Softworks. You're born in Vault 101 and raised through the years by your father James who is a brilliant scientist in the community...life is good and couldn't be any better. You're safe, you have many friends and everything that you need to survive and life goes on. That is until your nineteenth year when your beloved father inexplicably leaves the Vault without you or an explanation for his actions. With no time to process this loss, you have to react fast when the overly paranoid and controlling Overseer of the Vault locks it down and immediately sends his security force after you. Following a brief conflict you are able to get away from security with the aid of one of your closest childhood friends and flee the confines of the Vault. As you emerge from Vault 101 for the first time in your life you find yourself standing in what's left of a once thriving civilization at the height of it's technology now a decimated and nearly barren radioactive wasteland. It is here "Lone Wanderer" that your adventure begins as you start the search through the expansive and dangerous Capital Wasteland for your missing father. "Tick...tick...tickity!".

The gameplay of this title can be enjoyed in either a first or third person perspective. I for one tend to always go with the first person as it just seems more immersive for me but to each his or her own as they say. As with your typical R.P.G., you earn experience points for defeating enemies and completing various tasks and missions. Once you earn enough experience points your character then levels up which gives you access to a number of skill points which can then be applied to various attributes that you possess. These attributes or skills can range from anything like lockpicking, medicine, sneak to gunplay as well as a plethora of other choices. You have the option to mix and match skills as you see fit in order to create the type of character that you envision for this grand adventure. Also, as you reach certain experience levels you will be granted a choice of a perk which can greatly enhance and customize your characters abilities even further. When it comes to fighting, depending on how you choose to play the game, there are a number of different ways to approach combat in this title. You can choose to specialize in big or small guns and charge into battle shooting first and asking questions later. Perhaps you would like a more personal approach to combat by choosing melee and engaging your foes up close with unarmed combat tactics or brawler type weaponry istead. If stealth is your bailiwick then you could take down your foes from a distance with sniper rifles or set traps with mines for them to unsuspectingly set off. There are just a variety of options to take as far as combat is concerned which is a great incentive. Another terrific gameplay element in this title is the sense of immersion that you get as you travel about the Capital wasteland. The number of varied locations, weather conditions and time cycling from day to night...the title does an exceptional job of making you feel as though you are actually there. Over the course of the story you will also have a number of choices to make that will affect the world around you in various ways so choose wisely. In short, with the ample amount of people to interact with, a gorgeous expansive environment to explore, fascinating lore to discover and exciting combat, Fallout 3: Game Of The Year Edition delivers an amazing R.P.G. experience.

I for one still to this day love the visual style of this game even in it's basic vanilla form. It managed quite well to believably immerse me in a world devastated by a nuclear holocaust. From the destroyed infrastructure, horribly irradiated lifeforms to the interesting post-war people that you meet still trying to survive somehow? The developers managed to create a beautifully crafted world using mostly damaged and destroyed things if that makes any sense whatsoever...I guess you just have to see it for yourself? The character models look great, are quite varied and are nicely animated. The game also uses excellent lighting which you will notice as time transitions from day to night and vice versa. One thing that I have really liked about all the Fallout titles is how they manage to take things from the past along with things from the future and combine them to create a visual amalgam of the two that just, to quote someone at Bethesda, "...it just works!". In summary, presentation-wise Fallout 3: Game Of The Year Edition does a remarkable job of creating a visually pleasing post-apocalyptic world filled with an abundance of exciting locations to explore, believable people to interact with and terrifying opponents to battle.

Bear in mind that I never played the game until years after it's initial release but for me Fallout 3 was yet another masterpiece delivered from the developers at Bethesda Game Studios. Like the other games in their various franchises I completely loved this title and lost myself in this world that they created. This game suprised me with a sense of immersion that few titles ever had previously. I found the story compelling and tried to complete as many missions and sidequests as possible just to see what would happen next. I also really adored the character creator, attributes and perk system as well as the terrific combat but the absolute best thing about the title of course is the afformentioned sense of immersion that I got from playing. The freedom to go where you want to go and do what you choose to do was just so enjoyable which is why I always look forward to the next chapters in Bethesda's big franchise titles such as this. Whether you like them or hate them you do have to admit that they create some fascinating worlds to exist in and that alone is worth the price of admission for me. Also, replayability is very high for this title what with the expansive modding community available for Fallout 3 in the form of literally thousands of mods that will allow you to fine tune your game however you like. Sadly, there are no Steam Achievements or Steam Trading Cards to collect but there are game add-ons in the form of "Operation: Anchorage", "The Pitt", "Broken Steel", "Point Lookout" and "Mothership Zeta" which add many new and exciting locations to visit as well as missions to complete. In conclusion, Fallout 3: Game Of The Year Edition is simply one of those titles that every gamer, casual or hardcore, should have in their collection so it is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED as it will give you many wonderful hours of gameplay for the money spent.
